learning_goal: Describe the hip as a ball-and-socket joint, say which bony parts form the ball and the socket, name the muscle group that produces each of its six movements, explain why the joint is stable where the shoulder is not, and predict the deformity and the nerve at risk in a posterior dislocation.

structures.name: right hip bone
structures.label: Hip bone
structures.narration: All three parts of the hip bone build the socket: ilium above, ischium behind and below, pubis in front.

structures.label: Acetabulum
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: CONTACT — the socket is where the femur meets the hip bone (gaps 1.02mm · 1 witness)
structures.narration: The socket is the acetabulum. Its articular surface is a horseshoe called the lunate surface; the floor inside the horseshoe, the acetabular fossa, is not articular and holds fat. The rim is deepened all round by a fibrocartilaginous labrum, and the gap below is bridged by the transverse acetabular ligament.
structures.reviewed_note: opened in the 3D viewer and looked at: the patch lands on the feature the label names. Checked by Claude on 2026-08-28 at Frank’s request, not by an independent human reader — the measurement and its evidence are in calibrated_by.

structures.name: right femur
structures.label: Femur
structures.narration: The head sits on a neck that runs up and medially at about one hundred and twenty-five degrees to the shaft. That long neck is what gives the hip its range — and what makes it the classic fracture in an elderly patient.

structures.label: Head of femur
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: CONTACT — the ball is where the femur meets the hip bone (gaps 1.02mm · 1 witness)
structures.narration: The ball is the head of the femur, more than half a sphere. The small pit on it is the fovea, where the ligament of the head attaches.
structures.reviewed_note: opened in the 3D viewer and looked at: the patch lands on the feature the label names. Checked by Claude on 2026-08-28 at Frank’s request, not by an independent human reader — the measurement and its evidence are in calibrated_by.

structures.label: Greater trochanter
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: EXTREME -x within slab z:0.8,1.0 on FMA24474 (right femur, 440.2 mm, long axis z) — the most lateral point of the upper fifth of the bone. 559 vertices considered, 189.3 mm from the surface centroid.
structures.narration: The one part of this region you can put a finger on. Gluteus medius and minimus land here, the short lateral rotators reach its medial surface, and the line from the ischial tuberosity to this point is how beat 1 finds the joint from behind. The hollow on its medial side is the trochanteric fossa.

structures.label: Lesser trochanter
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: CONTACT — the nearest point on FMA24474 to FMA22342 (right psoas major), the muscle that inserts on it. Gap 0.87 mm, spread 0 mm, 1 witness — a measurement with no second witness, hence needs-review.
structures.narration: Where iliopsoas ends, on the back and medial side of the upper femur. It marks the lower limit of the neck: the intertrochanteric line in front runs down to it, so a fracture at this level is extracapsular and the head keeps its blood supply.

structures.name: sacrum
structures.label: Sacrum
structures.narration: Weight comes down the vertebral column into the sacrum, crosses the sacroiliac joint into the ilium, and is delivered to the acetabulum. Everything above the hip joint stands on these two bones meeting.

structures.name: right inguinal ligament
structures.label: Inguinal ligament
structures.narration: The front of the joint lies just below the middle of this ligament. That is where you feel the femoral pulse, and it is the surface marking a clinician uses to find the joint from outside.

structures.name: right psoas major
structures.label: Psoas major
structures.narration: The chief flexor. It comes from the lumbar vertebrae, crosses the front of the joint capsule, and ends on the lesser trochanter. A bursa separates its tendon from the capsule and often communicates with the joint — which is how a psoas abscess tracking down from the spine can present as a painful hip.

structures.name: right iliacus
structures.label: Iliacus
structures.narration: It fills the iliac fossa and joins the psoas tendon, so the two are usually taught as one muscle, iliopsoas. Femoral nerve, L2 and L3.

structures.name: right rectus femoris
structures.label: Rectus femoris
structures.narration: The only part of quadriceps that crosses the hip. Its straight head takes origin from the anterior inferior iliac spine and its reflected head from the rim of the acetabulum itself, so a strip of it is attached to the socket.

structures.name: right sartorius
structures.label: Sartorius
structures.narration: The longest muscle in the body, running from the anterior superior iliac spine across the thigh to the medial side of the tibia. At the hip it flexes, abducts and laterally rotates all at once — the position a tailor sits in, which is where its name comes from.

structures.name: right pectineus
structures.label: Pectineus
structures.narration: A flat square muscle on the floor of the femoral triangle that both flexes and adducts. It sits on the boundary between the two nerve territories and is often supplied by both the femoral and the obturator nerve.

structures.name: right tensor fasciae latae
structures.label: Tensor fasciae latae
structures.narration: It abducts and medially rotates the hip and steadies the trunk on the standing leg. Superior gluteal nerve, like the two gluteal abductors behind it.

structures.name: right gluteus medius
structures.label: Gluteus medius
structures.narration: The main abductor. Its real job is not lifting the leg sideways but holding the pelvis level when you stand on one leg. Weakness here drops the opposite side of the pelvis with every step.

structures.name: right gluteus minimus
structures.label: Gluteus minimus
structures.narration: The same action again, deep to medius, and it lies directly on the capsule of the joint. Both abductors are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve and both medially rotate the hip.

structures.name: right adductor longus
structures.label: Adductor longus
structures.narration: The most anterior adductor and the one you can feel as a cord in the groin. Obturator nerve, like the rest of this group.

structures.name: right adductor brevis
structures.label: Adductor brevis
structures.narration: It lies behind longus, and the two divisions of the obturator nerve split around it — one in front of it, one behind. That relationship is a favourite question.

structures.name: right adductor magnus
structures.label: Adductor magnus
structures.narration: The biggest of the group and a hybrid: its adductor part is obturator nerve, its hamstring part is sciatic. So it both adducts and extends the hip, on two different nerves.

structures.name: right gracilis
structures.label: Gracilis
structures.narration: The strap on the inner edge of the thigh. It is the only adductor that crosses the knee as well as the hip.

structures.name: right gluteus maximus
structures.label: Gluteus maximus
structures.narration: The powerful extensor, used for climbing and rising rather than level walking. It also rotates the hip laterally, and it covers the whole back of the joint.

structures.name: long head of right biceps femoris
structures.label: Biceps femoris — long head
structures.narration: Hamstrings extend the hip in ordinary walking. All three arise from the ischial tuberosity, which sits just below and behind the joint.

structures.name: right semitendinosus
structures.label: Semitendinosus
structures.narration: A long tendon on the medial side, running to the pes anserinus on the tibia.

structures.name: right semimembranosus
structures.label: Semimembranosus
structures.narration: The deepest hamstring, membranous above and tendinous below.

structures.name: right piriformis
structures.label: Piriformis
structures.narration: It runs out of the pelvis and across the back of the joint to the top of the greater trochanter. The sciatic nerve appears just below it, which is why a posterior dislocation of the hip threatens that nerve.

structures.name: right gemellus superior
structures.label: Gemellus superior
structures.narration: Upper twin, from the ischial spine.

structures.name: right obturator internus
structures.label: Obturator internus
structures.narration: It begins inside the pelvis, turns a right angle round the lesser sciatic notch, and reaches the medial surface of the greater trochanter with a twin above and below it.

structures.name: right gemellus inferior
structures.label: Gemellus inferior
structures.narration: Lower twin, from the upper part of the ischial tuberosity.

structures.name: right quadratus femoris
structures.label: Quadratus femoris
structures.narration: Flat and square, from the ischial tuberosity to the back of the femur. The sciatic nerve lies directly on it as it leaves the buttock.

structures.name: right obturator externus
structures.label: Obturator externus
structures.narration: The one that goes underneath. Its tendon winds below the neck of the femur to reach the trochanteric fossa, so it is the only one of the group that reaches the femur from below the neck rather than crossing straight across the back of the joint. Obturator nerve, not sciatic — the odd one out of the group.

views.title: Find the joint
views.narration: The hip joint is buried. Muscle covers it on every side, so you can never see it or feel it directly on a patient. You locate it instead: about two centimetres below the midpoint of the inguinal ligament in front, and midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter behind. The marker lit on the femur is that trochanter — the only bony point of this region you can actually find through the skin.

views.title: Two bones, one socket
views.narration: Strip the muscle away and the joint is simple: a spherical head sitting in a deep cup. This is a synovial ball-and-socket joint of the multiaxial type, so it moves in three planes. Compare it with the shoulder, where the socket is a shallow saucer. Here the cup holds more than half the ball, and that single fact explains everything about hip stability.

views.title: Cut through the ball and socket
views.narration: Drag the plane through the joint. Inside, the horseshoe-shaped lunate surface carries the load; the fossa in its centre is filled with fat and the ligament of the head. Cartilage covers the head everywhere except at the fovea. The fibrocartilaginous labrum on the rim grips past the equator of the head, so the joint holds the head in even before any muscle acts.

views.title: Where the capsule ends
views.narration: The two markers are the ends of the argument: the head above, the lesser trochanter below. The capsule runs from the acetabular rim to the intertrochanteric line in front, but behind it stops halfway along the neck. So the whole neck is inside the capsule in front and only the medial half behind. That line is the difference between an intracapsular and an extracapsular fracture, and therefore between a neck that loses its blood supply and one that does not.

views.title: The ligaments that stop you falling backwards
views.narration: Three ligaments thicken the capsule, all spiralling in the same direction. The iliofemoral ligament in front is an inverted Y and the strongest ligament in the body; the pubofemoral is below and in front; the ischiofemoral is behind. Standing upright pushes the pelvis backwards, all three wind tight, and the hip locks with no muscular effort. That is why you can stand all day without tiring your hip.

views.title: Weight goes through here
views.narration: Follow the load. Body weight comes down the vertebral column into the sacrum, through the sacroiliac joint into the ilium, and reaches the acetabulum along a thickened strut of bone. It crosses into the head of the femur and turns a corner down the neck to the shaft. Standing on one leg, the force across this joint is around three times body weight; running, it is far more. The joint is built for load first and movement second.

views.title: Flexion and extension
views.narration: In front, the flexors: iliopsoas chiefly, helped by rectus femoris, sartorius and pectineus. Behind, the extensors: hamstrings for ordinary walking, gluteus maximus for power. Flexion reaches about one hundred and twenty degrees with the knee bent, but far less with the knee straight, because the hamstrings run out of length. Extension is only about twenty degrees, checked by the iliofemoral ligament.

views.title: Abduction and adduction
views.narration: Laterally, gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae abduct, all on the superior gluteal nerve. Medially, the adductor group pulls the other way, all on the obturator nerve. Learn the pair as two nerves rather than two lists: superior gluteal abducts, obturator adducts. The abductors matter more clinically, because they are what keeps the pelvis level in single-leg stance.

views.title: Rotation, and the muscle that goes under the neck
views.narration: Six short muscles rotate the hip laterally: piriformis, gemellus superior, obturator internus, gemellus inferior, quadratus femoris and obturator externus. Five of them cross behind the joint. Obturator externus is the exception — highlighted here — winding under the neck of the femur to the trochanteric fossa, and supplied by the obturator nerve while the others are not. Medial rotation has no dedicated muscle at all; it is done by gluteus minimus, the front fibres of gluteus medius and tensor fasciae latae, which is why medial rotation is the weakest movement of the hip.

views.title: What lies against the capsule
views.narration: Learn the joint's neighbours by side. In front, iliopsoas with its bursa, and beyond it the femoral nerve, artery and vein in the femoral triangle. Above, the reflected head of rectus femoris and gluteus minimus lying straight on the capsule. Behind, piriformis and the short rotators, and on them the sciatic nerve. Below, obturator externus and the obturator nerve. Every one of these is a route by which hip disease refers pain somewhere else.

views.title: Posterior dislocation
views.narration: Dislocation needs great force, and nine times out of ten it goes backwards. The classic setting is a dashboard injury: the hip flexed and adducted when the knee strikes, so the head is driven out behind the acetabulum. The leg then lies shortened, adducted and medially rotated — the picture to recognise in an exam. The traced path is the sciatic nerve passing right behind the joint; it is injured in about one dislocation in ten, and the foot drop that follows is the reason you always test dorsiflexion afterwards.

views.title: Why the hip hurts at the knee
views.narration: The capsule is supplied by branches of the femoral, obturator and sciatic nerves — and the same three nerves supply the knee. So a child with hip disease often complains only of knee pain, and a normal knee examination does not exclude a hip problem. Always examine the joint above.

views.title: Peel down to the joint
views.narration: Recite the approach: skin and fascia, then the outer muscular sleeve, then the deeper rotators and abductors lying on the capsule, then the capsule and its three spiral ligaments, then the labrum, then the head in the socket. Five layers, and after this the hip should feel like a place with an address rather than a name in a list.

gaps: The catalog holds no capsule or ligament of the hip. The iliofemoral, pubofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments carry most of the joint's stability and two whole beats turn on them, but they can only be narrated against the bones and shown with a relationship connector.

There is no acetabular labrum, no transverse acetabular ligament and no ligament of the head of the femur in the catalog, so the deepening of the socket and the fovea are taught by cutting the bone models and describing what would be there.
No articular cartilage is modelled, so the lunate surface and the non-articular acetabular fossa are shown as bone shape only.

The head, neck and trochanters are features of the whole femur mesh rather than separate models. Three of the four are now measured landmark anchors on FMA24474 rather than a lit whole bone: the head (contact with the hip bone), the greater trochanter (most lateral point of the upper fifth) and the lesser trochanter (contact with psoas major). All three are single-witness measurements and carry status 'needs-review'. The NECK is not authored and should not be: a neck is a narrowest cross-section, which is neither of derive-landmark.mjs's two definitions, and the same finding was recorded in the radius-ulna scene. It is still taught by lighting the femur and naming it.

No nerve of the lower limb exists as a model. The sciatic nerve behind the joint is authored as a traced concept path across piriformis and quadratus femoris, and the femoral and obturator nerves are taught by lighting the muscles they supply.
No artery of the lower limb is modelled, so the blood supply of the head of the femur is not shown here at all. It is taught in the Proximal femur scene, which this scene does not claim to cover.
The psoas bursa is described but has no model, so its communication with the joint cavity is narration only.
This scene does not cover Proximal femur, Sciatic nerve or Gluteal vessels.
